title: Continuity And Differentiability Of Saddle-functions
notes: Begin by fixing the sign convention before any theorem names appear. In this section K is concave in the u variable and convex in the v variable. That means the first partial certificate behaves like a supergradient, the second like an ordinary convex subgradient, and the combined saddle mapping has two different monotonicity signs.

title: Compact Continuity Transfer
notes: Present the first theorem as a transfer principle rather than a surprise. A finite convex function is locally Lipschitz on compact cores of its domain, and the saddle case repeats that argument twice: once with v fixed and once with u fixed. The visual box reminds students that the constants are only promised on an interior compact rectangle.

title: Families Stay Equi-Lipschitz
notes: The family theorem is the workhorse behind the later convergence statements. Pointwise boundedness on a sufficiently spanning sample set is not merely a weak data condition; through convexity in one direction and concavity in the other, it propagates to uniform bounds and a common Lipschitz constant on every compact box.

title: Dense Data Determines Limits
notes: This slide bundles the continuity in a parameter, dense-set convergence, and subsequence compactness results. The message is operational: if a sequence of finite saddle-functions is controlled on dense product data, the compact Lipschitz theorem prevents hidden oscillation between sample points. Uniform convergence on compact sets is what lets later derivative statements pass to limits.

title: Directional Derivative Splits
notes: The joint directional derivative is the first genuinely saddle-specific moment. The theorem says that at an interior finite point, moving simultaneously in u and v has the same first-order effect as adding the u-only and v-only directional effects. The proof idea is a two-leg path plus continuity, and the diagram gives that path a geometric form.

title: Partial Subgradient Certificates
notes: Now translate derivatives into certificates. On the concave u side, the affine plane lies above the slice, so the displayed inequality has the reverse direction from the usual convex subgradient inequality. On the convex v side, the affine plane lies below. The product of these two certificate sets is the saddle subdifferential.

title: Derivative As A Support Test
notes: At an interior point of a proper saddle-function, the partial subgradient sets are nonempty, closed, bounded, and convex. Directional derivatives can then be read from the extreme pairings with these sets: an infimum on the concave side and a supremum on the convex side. The rectangle is a synthetic model of that product set.

title: Outer Continuity Of The Saddle Mapping
notes: The continuity theorem for the subdifferential should be heard as an outer-continuity statement. Nearby saddle subgradients cannot suddenly escape far outside the old subgradient set plus a small ball. The one-sided semicontinuity of the directional derivatives is the scalar shadow of this set-valued containment.

title: Differentiability Means Singleton Mapping
notes: The differentiability theorem has two directions. If K is differentiable, the gradient is the only possible saddle subgradient. Conversely, if the product subdifferential contains exactly one vector pair, separate differentiability follows from the one-variable theory, and the saddle convergence theorem upgrades that to joint differentiability.

title: Linearity Is The Directional Test
notes: The corollary gives a fast diagnostic: near a finite point, differentiability is equivalent to the directional derivative being a linear function of the direction. It is enough to have all two-sided partial derivatives finite, because the split directional derivative then cannot keep a kink in any coordinate direction.

title: Smooth Points Are Almost Everywhere
notes: The full-measure theorem says nonsmoothness is thin even for saddle-functions. Along each coordinate line, a one-dimensional convex derivative can only have finitely many large jumps on a bounded interval. Taking countable jump thresholds and finitely many coordinates leaves a dense differentiability set whose gradient map is continuous on that set.

title: Gradients Converge With The Functions
notes: The last theorem is a stability result. When differentiable finite saddle-functions converge pointwise to a differentiable finite saddle-function, compact convergence of the functions and continuity of the limiting gradient force the gradients to converge uniformly on compact sets. This is the saddle analogue of the smooth convex convergence theorem from the differential theory.

title: Quadratic Saddle Lab
notes: Use the quadratic lab to connect the abstract signs to numbers. For K equal to minus one half u squared plus uv plus one half v squared, the u-side pairing is nonpositive because the u slice is concave, while the v-side pairing is nonnegative because the v slice is convex. The notebook check is exactly this sign discipline in sampled form.

title: Rule Ledger
notes: Close by asking students to name the tests in order: compact continuity, equi-Lipschitz family control, dense-set convergence, split directional derivatives, partial subgradient certificates, singleton differentiability, almost-everywhere smoothness, and gradient convergence. The section is a bridge from ordinary convex regularity to saddle mappings.
